docs.title: The Robot PC in simulation, in two commands
docs.text:
No board and no arm are needed: the Robot PC runs ros2_control with mock hardware in Docker, on a network that stands in for the Wi-Fi link to the Operator PC. A second container on the same network checks it over ROS 2 DDS.

git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot.git
cd sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up --build robot_pc                 # terminal 1: the Robot PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh    # terminal 2: a second host

The smoke test passes when it receives /joint_states, finds the joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller active, and arm_controller executes a short trajectory. In VS Code, Ctrl+Shift+B offers the same steps as tasks (Getting started).

docs.title: Connection guide for beginners
docs.text:
This page is for readers who want to work on robotics algorithms — motion planning, kinematics, control, trajectories — and are not (yet) at home in electronics. It shows in pictures what is connected to what, in three levels. You can stop at any level: everything above level 1 is optional.

SmartManipulator-X is part of the SystemFromScratch® portfolio and is also meant for teaching. All parts are open source: this Robot PC repository, the Operator PC and the doppelstep drive firmware (documentation) are published under the Apache License 2.0. Use them, study them, change them.

Educational material, at your own risk

This guide is provided as is, without warranty (Apache License 2.0, sections 7 and 8). Levels 2 and 3 use mains-powered supplies, 24 V and moving mechanics. You build and power the hardware at your own risk: follow the safety rules and, if you are unsure, ask someone experienced to check your wiring before the first power-up.

Status (2026-11-15): level 1 works today. Levels 2 and 3 describe the planned hardware (project status); the pictures are the target to build towards. The drawings are simplified: on a real board, follow the labels printed next to the pads.

docs.title: The three levels at a glance
docs.text: Level What you need What you can do State 1 · Simulation One computer with Docker Plan and execute arm motions, write ROS 2 nodes, test algorithms against simulated joints Works 2 · One joint on the desk Level 1 + one drive board, one stepper motor, a lab supply, a USB cable Run your trajectories on a real motor, see real timing and limits Planned (Stage 2) 3 · The whole robot The arm, six drives, the Robot PC board, supplies, a small interface circuit Run your algorithms on the real arm Planned (Stages 3–4)

docs.title: Level 1: everything on one computer
docs.text:
Level 1: one computer runs the Operator PC and the Robot PC in Docker; no cables and no boards

Nothing to connect. Two Docker containers play the two computers of the real system: the Operator PC plans motions (MoveIt 2, RViz2), the Robot PC executes them with simulated joints. They talk over ROS 2 exactly as they will over Wi-Fi on the real robot, so code written here is built to run on the real arm without changes.

Start with Getting started. The interface your algorithms use — joint names, topics, controllers — is the joint contract of the Robot PC.

One step further, still without hardware: in the tutorial: the whole robot in simulation you move the arm from RViz2, and six simulated doppelstep drives carry out the motion with the same Robot PC software that will run on the arm. It assumes no experience with Linux, Docker or ROS.

docs.title: Level 2: one joint on the desk
docs.text:
Level 2: the computer connects to one drive with a USB cable; the motor has four wires to U, V and W; a lab supply powers the drive

The smallest real hardware: one drive board (an ST B-G431B-ESC1 running the doppelstep firmware) and one stepper motor. To your computer the drive looks like a ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL smart servo, so the same Robot PC software drives it.

  1. USB cable from your computer to the micro-USB socket of the drive. It carries the commands, the firmware update and the log.
  2. Motor, four wires. A stepper motor has two coils (A and B). Find which two wires belong together with a multimeter (a few ohms between the two wires of one coil, nothing between different coils). Then: A+ to U, B+ to V, A− and B− together to W.
  3. Supply last. A laboratory power supply at 12 V with the current limit set low (about 0.5 A) to the + and − pads. Red is +, black is −.

Before the first motor turns, the drive needs a one-time check described in the doppelstep bring-up checklist.

docs.title: Level 3: the whole robot
docs.text:
Level 3: Operator laptop over Wi-Fi to the CM4-Duino; a breadboard interface; a two-wire bus to six drives, each with its motor; a 24 V supply through the E-stop and a fuse; a USB-C adapter for the CM4-Duino

Read the picture from top to bottom:

  • Operator laptop — your computer with MoveIt 2 and your algorithms. It reaches the robot over Wi-Fi; no cable.
  • CM4-Duino — the Robot PC on the robot: a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 on a small carrier board. It has its own USB-C power adapter (5 V).
  • Bus interface — three tiny logic chips on a breadboard that turn the two UART pins of the CM4 into the single-wire bus of the drives.
  • The bus — just two wires (DATA and GND, twisted together) from the interface to every drive. Each drive has its own number (ID 1–6), so one pair of wires reaches all of them.
  • Six drives with six motors — one drive per motor; the shoulder has two motors.
  • 24 V supply — powers the motors through an emergency stop button and a fuse. A small converter makes 6 V for the gripper servo (a later project).

docs.title: Close-up: the CM4-Duino and the bus interface
docs.text:
CM4-Duino close-up: jumper wires from D14, D15, 3V3 and GND to the breadboard; two wires DATA and GND to the drives

Four jumper wires go from the CM4-Duino to the breadboard: D14 (send), D15 (receive), 3V3 (power for the chips) and GND. The circuit and the part numbers are on the Wiring page. The chips come in very small packages; solder each onto a small SOT-23-to-DIP adapter board so it fits the breadboard.

docs.title: Close-up: one drive
docs.text:
Drive close-up: motor wires to U, V, W; +24 V and ground to the + and − pads; bus DATA to J3 pin 2 and bus GND to J3 pin 5

Every drive gets the same eight wires: four from its motor, two from the 24 V supply, two from the bus (J3 pin 2 = DATA, J3 pin 5 = GND). The other J3 pins stay free, and the USB socket stays unplugged on the robot.

docs.text: Word Meaning here Bus One pair of wires shared by several devices; each answers only to its own ID DATA / GND The two bus wires: the signal, and the common reference (ground) Ground (GND, −) The 0 V reference. All grounds of the system meet at one point Drive The board that turns commands into motor current Coil A stepper motor has two; each has two wires Supply (PSU) Turns mains into 24 V (motors) or 5 V (CM4-Duino) DC/DC converter Turns one DC voltage into another (24 V to 6 V for the servo) E-stop A big red button that cuts motor power immediately DYNAMIXEL A family of ROBOTIS smart servos; our drives speak their protocol

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
1. Connect and disconnect wires only with all supplies off. A stepper unplugged while powered can destroy its drive.
  2. Check every connection with the multimeter before the first power-up: no short between + and −.
  3. First power-up on a lab supply with a low current limit; the 24 V supply only when everything works.
  4. Keep the emergency stop within reach and hands out of the arm's reach while it moves.
  5. The logic pins of the CM4-Duino accept only 3.3 V: never connect 5 V or 24 V to them.

docs.title: Robot PC image
docs.text:
The image is based on ros:jazzy-ros-base. It imports the DYNAMIXEL SDK and interface packages through ros2_robot.repos, builds them together with the project packages, and contains ROS control, USB diagnostics and build tools. MoveIt 2, RViz2, Gazebo and the OpenMANIPULATOR GUI and bringup packages are deliberately excluded: they belong to the Operator PC.

The workspace is baked into the image, not bind-mounted, so rebuild after changing project sources or ros2_robot.repos:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml build robot_pc
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml build --no-cache --pull robot_pc   # from scratch

The jazzy refs in ros2_robot.repos are branch names and can move; pin immutable revisions before relying on a build for verification.

.vscode/tasks.json runs Docker Compose from the repository root. Ctrl+Shift+B opens a picker with every task of the build group; none is the default, so the picker always appears.

Task Group Command Robot PC: Start (mock hardware) build docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up --build robot_pc Robot PC: Start (SIL, simulated doppelstep drives) build up --build robot_pc with docker/docker-compose.sil.yml Tests: Virtual DYNAMIXEL bus test python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/sim/tests -v Robot PC: Stop build docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml down Robot PC: Rebuild and restart build Stop, then up --build --force-recreate robot_pc Robot PC: Build image build build robot_pc Robot PC: Rebuild image (no cache) build build --no-cache --pull robot_pc Docs: Build PDF manual build python tools/docs/build_manual.py in .venv Robot PC: Smoke test (probe) test run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh Robot PC: Probe shell – run --rm probe bash Docs: Live preview – mkdocs serve in .venv

docs.title: Robot description from the CAD
docs.text:
smartmanipulator_x_description is generated from a STEP export of the BCN3D Moveo assembly by the scripts in tools/cad/ (Python 3 with numpy, scipy and matplotlib). The STEP itself is not in the repository (about 200 MB):

tools/cad/run_all.sh BCN3D_Moveo_assembly.stp ../BCN3D-Moveo /tmp/smx_cad

The steps, the measured dimensions and the conventions of the model are in tools/cad/README.md and on the BCN3D Moveo mechanics page.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is the Markdown in docs/. MkDocs Material turns it into the website, and tools/docs/build_manual.py turns the same pages into the printable A4 user manual (cover, imprint, contents with page numbers, numbered chapters, running headers, PDF bookmarks), rendered with WeasyPrint. Both follow the SystemFromScratch® documentation style; the landing page is configured in mkdocs.yml → extra.landing and the manual in mkdocs.yml → extra.manual.

Set up the tools once in the repository .venv. WeasyPrint needs the Pango library: on Windows from MSYS2 (pacman -S mingw-w64-x86_64-pango; the builder finds C:\msys64\mingw64\bin by itself), on Ubuntu apt install libpango-1.0-0 libpangoft2-1.0-0.

# Windows (PowerShell, repository root)
py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt

# Linux (repository root)
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
Command Result python -m mkdocs serve Live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 python -m mkdocs build Static website in site/ (strict: a broken link fails the build) python tools/docs/build_manual.py build/manual/SmartManipulator-X_User_Manual_v<version>.pdf; the version is the latest vX.Y.Z tag python tools/docs/build_manual.py --output docs/downloads/SmartManipulator-X_User_Manual.pdf The file the website links to (CI does this before deploying) python tools/docs/diagrams.py Regenerates the hero illustration docs/assets/images/hero-3d.svg; the arm is drawn from the robot description meshes and URDF by tools/docs/hero_robot.py, so run it again after the description changes python tools/docs/pictorial_diagrams.py Regenerates the pictorial connection views docs/hardware/images/pictorial-*.svg of the beginners' guide python tools/docs/wiring_diagrams.py Regenerates the wiring diagrams docs/hardware/images/wiring-*.svg; pin names must match the Wiring page python tools/docs/render_mermaid.py Renders docs/**/diagrams/*.mmd to docs/**/images/*.svg (needs Playwright and a network connection; no Mermaid sources at the moment)

Writing rules that keep the website and the PDF correct:

  • Start every page with exactly one # Title; chapter and section numbers are added in the PDF, so do not number headings by hand.
  • Add a new page to nav in mkdocs.yml, otherwise it is missing from the site and the PDF.
  • An image on a line of its own, ![Caption](images/file.svg), becomes a figure with its alt text as the caption (tools/docs/hooks.py).
  • Link to other pages with relative .md paths; strict mode checks them, and the PDF turns them into page references.
  • Third-party documents (datasheets, vendor schematics, photos, 3D models, example code) are not ours to redistribute. Keep a backup copy in the repository (docs/hardware/datasheets/, docs/hardware/cm4-duino/vendor/), exclude that folder from the website with exclude_docs in mkdocs.yml, and link to the original on the publisher's website, with the date the link was checked and the backup path as plain text for when the link breaks.
  • Diagrams are SVG files generated by the scripts above; never edit them by hand. The PDF renderer runs no JavaScript, so a Mermaid diagram needs its source in diagrams/*.mmd next to the page, rendered with render_mermaid.py (no page uses Mermaid at the moment).

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide takes you from a fresh clone of the Robot PC repository to a running Robot PC in simulation, checked from a second ROS 2 host. No drive and no arm are needed: ros2_control runs with mock hardware, where every commanded joint position becomes the joint state at once.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Where What Simulation (any computer) Git, Docker Engine or Docker Desktop (Windows with the WSL 2 backend works) and Docker Compose v2 Real hardware Not usable yet: the real-hardware path is planned, see the project status. It will need a Linux Docker host with a doppelstep drive on a serial port, or the CM4-Duino Optional VS Code, which runs every step below as a task

ROS 2 is not installed on the host: it comes with the Robot PC image (ros:jazzy-ros-base).

docs.title: Clone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot.git
cd sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot

docs.title: Start the Robot PC
docs.text:
From the repository root:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up --build robot_pc

The first run builds the image, which takes several minutes. The Compose file creates the Docker network smx_net (10.77.0.0/24), which stands in for the network link (Wi-Fi on the robot) between the Robot PC and the Operator PC, and starts the Robot PC container at 10.77.0.10. It runs robot_state_publisher, ros2_control_node with mock hardware, joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller. The logs stay in the terminal.

docs.title: Check it from a second host
docs.text:
In a second terminal, start the probe container on the same network and run the smoke test:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh

The test passes when it receives /joint_states, finds joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller active, and arm_controller executes a short trajectory. For your own ros2 commands, open a shell on the probe instead:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe bash
ros2 topic list

Any other container on smx_net with the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID (default 42) sees the Robot PC through ROS 2 DDS like a second machine on the LAN. To change the domain, the subnet or the image tag, copy docker/env.example to docker/.env.

docs.title: Stop and rebuild
docs.text:
Stop with Ctrl+C in the first terminal, or remove the containers and the network:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml down

The workspace is built into the image, not mounted. After changing project sources or ros2_robot.repos, start with up --build again.

docs.title: The same steps in VS Code
docs.text:
Ctrl+Shift+B opens the build task picker:

Task Does Robot PC: Start (mock hardware) up --build robot_pc; the logs stay in a dedicated terminal Robot PC: Stop down: removes the containers and smx_net Robot PC: Rebuild and restart Stop, then up --build --force-recreate robot_pc Robot PC: Build image Builds the image without starting it Robot PC: Rebuild image (no cache) Full rebuild, pulls the base image again Docs: Build PDF manual Writes the PDF user manual (see Development)

The smoke test is under Tasks: Run Test Task, the probe shell and the documentation preview under Tasks: Run Task.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SmartManipulator-X is a robot arm project. It combines the ROS 2 control and operator-software concepts of ROBOTIS OpenMANIPULATOR-X with the mechanical design of BCN3D Moveo. Instead of DYNAMIXEL actuators, every stepper joint of the Moveo has a doppelstep drive that answers on a DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 bus as an XM430-W350 servo. The Robot PC, a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 on a CM4-Duino board, runs the unchanged ROBOTIS host software as the bus master. The ROBOTIS stack can then drive the arm as if it were built from DYNAMIXEL servos.

This documentation covers the whole system: the Robot PC and its board, the DYNAMIXEL bus and the drives, the shared device contract, the Operator PC, and the mechanics. It is published from the Robot PC repository and is the starting point for all work on the project.

SmartManipulator-X system: Operator PC, Robot PC on the CM4-Duino, DYNAMIXEL bus, six doppelstep drives, gripper and Moveo mechanics

docs.title: Open source and education
docs.text: SmartManipulator-X is part of the SystemFromScratch® portfolio and is also built for teaching: from ROS 2 motion planning down to the current loop of a stepper drive, every layer is visible and documented. All parts are open source under the Apache License 2.0 — the Robot PC (this repository), the Operator PC and the doppelstep drive firmware. Readers who mainly want to work on algorithms start with the connection guide for beginners: the whole software stack runs in simulation on one computer, and the hardware can be added step by step.

docs.title: Tutorial: the whole robot in simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial is for you if you have never worked with ROS, Docker or Linux. At the end you move the SmartManipulator-X arm on your screen with the mouse, and the motion is carried out by the real software of the robot: the motion planner, the robot computer and the firmware of six motor drives. Only the motors themselves are simulated.

You need no electronics, only a computer. Every command is given in full: copy it, paste it, press Enter.

Time: about one hour the first time (mostly waiting for downloads), about five minutes every time after that.

docs.title: What you will start
docs.text:
The real robot consists of three kinds of parts. In this tutorial all of them run on your computer, each in its own box (a container):

 Operator PC                    Robot PC                         Six drives (doppelstep)
 MoveIt 2 + RViz2               ros2_control                     firmware of the motor drives
 "where should the arm go?" --> "move each joint like this" ---> "turn the motor"
 you click here                 virtual DYNAMIXEL bus  <-------  answer: "I am here now"
Part On the real robot In this tutorial Operator PC your laptop a container with MoveIt 2 (plans motions) and RViz2 (the window you click in) Robot PC a small computer on the robot (CM4-Duino) a container with ros2_control (turns a motion into commands for every joint) Drives six boards, one per motor six containers, each running the unchanged drive firmware; the motor is a computer model

docs.title: Words used here
docs.text: Word Meaning Terminal A window in which you type commands. Here always the Ubuntu terminal, never PowerShell WSL Windows Subsystem for Linux: a Linux (Ubuntu) inside Windows Docker Runs programs in containers: boxes with everything a program needs, so you install nothing else Image The template of a container. It is built (or downloaded) once, then started many times Repository A project folder with its full history, downloaded with git clone ROS 2 The robot software framework; the Operator PC and the Robot PC talk through it

docs.title: A1. Install WSL with Ubuntu
docs.text:
On Linux you can skip this step. On Windows 10 or 11:

  1. Right-click the Start button and open Terminal (Admin) or Windows PowerShell (Admin).

  2. Type:

    wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

  3. Restart the computer when asked. After the restart an Ubuntu window opens and asks for a user name and a password. Choose both and remember the password: Ubuntu asks for it when you install something. While you type it, nothing appears; that is normal.

Check it in PowerShell:

wsl --version

The output must contain a line WSLg version. If the command is unknown, your WSL is too old: run wsl --update and try again.

How to open the Ubuntu terminal later

Press the Windows key, type Ubuntu and open Ubuntu 24.04. In it, paste with right-click or Ctrl+Shift+V (Ctrl+V does not work there).

docs.title: A2. Install Docker Desktop
docs.text:
1. Download Docker Desktop from docker.com and install it with the default settings (keep Use WSL 2 switched on).
  2. Start Docker Desktop. Open Settings → Resources → WSL integration, switch on Ubuntu-24.04, then Apply & restart.

  3. Close the Ubuntu terminal and open a new one. Check:

    docker version

    The output must contain a Client part and a Server part. If it says docker: command not found, repeat step 2.

Docker Desktop must be running whenever you use the robot software (its whale icon is in the taskbar).

docs.title: A3. Download the three repositories
docs.text:
In the Ubuntu terminal:

mkdir -p ~/smx
cd ~/smx
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-doppelstep.git doppelstep
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot.git SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-operator.git SmartManipulator-X-Operator-PC
ls

ls must list three folders: doppelstep, SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC and SmartManipulator-X-Operator-PC. Keep exactly these names: the Operator PC looks for the Robot PC folder next to it under that name.

Why in Ubuntu and not on drive C:

Folders in Ubuntu (~ is your Ubuntu home folder) are much faster for Docker than folders on the Windows drive, and the files keep Linux line endings.

docs.title: A4. Let RViz2 open its window
docs.text:
RViz2 runs inside a container and has to reach your screen. Create a small settings file for the Operator PC:

cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Operator-PC
printf 'SMX_X11_DIR=/mnt/wslg/.X11-unix\nSMX_WSLG_DIR=/mnt/wslg\n' > docker/.env
cat docker/.env
ls /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix

cat shows the two lines you wrote; the last command must show X0. This works on Windows 10 and 11, as long as you start the Operator PC from the Ubuntu terminal.

On a Linux desktop use the X11 settings instead, described in the Operator PC documentation under GUI on a Linux desktop.

docs.title: A5. Build the drive firmware
docs.text:
The drive firmware is built once with the Zephyr tools, which come in their own image. This is the longest step (several gigabytes to download):

cd ~/smx/doppelstep
docker compose build
docker compose run --rm zephyr bash scripts/west-init.sh
docker compose run --rm zephyr west build -b native_sim/native/64 -s app -d build-native
ls build-native/zephyr/zephyr.exe

Expected: the last line prints build-native/zephyr/zephyr.exe. That file is the drive firmware as a Linux program.

The Robot PC and the Operator PC images are built automatically the first time you start them in Part B.

docs.title: Part B: start the robot (every time)
docs.text:
You need four Ubuntu terminals side by side. Open them now (Windows key, Ubuntu 24.04, four times) and give each one its job:

Terminal Job Stays open with a running log 1 the six drives no, it finishes at once 2 Robot PC yes 3 Operator PC with RViz2 yes 4 checks no

docs.title: B1. Terminal 1: start the six drives
docs.text:
cd ~/smx/doppelstep
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  docker compose run -d --rm --name dxl$i -p $((5554+i)):5555 zephyr \
    python3 tools/sim/run_native.py run --tcp 5555 --link /tmp/ttyDXL -- --flash=/tmp/flash.bin
done
docker ps --filter name=dxl --format '{{.Names}}  {{.Status}}'

Expected: six lines dxl1 … dxl6 Up …. The drives now run in the background. They all start with the factory ID 1; the Robot PC gives each one its own ID in the next step.

If you see The container name "/dxl1" is already in use, the drives still run from last time. That is fine: go on with B2.

docs.title: B2. Terminal 2: start the Robot PC
docs.text:
cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml up --build robot_pc

The first time this builds the image (10–20 minutes). Then the log scrolls. Wait for this line:

Configured and activated gripper_controller

Leave the terminal open. On the way you see ten lines FastSyncRead TxRx failed (attempt n/10): that is expected (the Robot PC tries a faster read mode first; with several drives on one bus they do not answer it, so it switches to the normal one, in which the drives answer one after the other).

docs.title: B3. Terminal 4: check that the Robot PC works
docs.text:
cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh

The test moves the arm a little and back, through the drives. Expected: PASS on the last line. If it fails, see When something goes wrong.

docs.title: B4. Terminal 3: start the Operator PC
docs.text:
cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Operator-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up --build operator_pc

The first time this builds the image (10–20 minutes). Wait for the line You can start planning now!. A window RViz opens on your Windows desktop (sometimes behind the other windows: look in the taskbar):

RViz2 after start: on the left the MotionPlanning panel with the Planning tab, Planning Group arm and the Goal State list; on the right the arm standing upright

docs.title: Part C: move the arm
docs.text:
In RViz, on the Planning tab of the MotionPlanning panel:

  1. Planning Group: arm (already selected).
  2. Goal State: open the list and choose ready. An orange arm shows where the arm should go; the grey arm is where it is now.
  3. Click Plan & Execute.

The arm bends forward. It moves slowly on purpose (Velocity Scaling 0.10). What happened: MoveIt planned a path without collisions, the Robot PC turned it into commands for every joint, and the six drive firmwares followed them and reported their positions back.

Now choose Goal State: home and click Plan & Execute again: the arm stands up.

Things to try next:

  • Drag the coloured arrows at the gripper to set your own goal, then Plan & Execute. If the orange arm stops following, the goal is out of reach.
  • Set Planning Group to gripper and choose closed or open. (The gripper is not driven by a doppelstep drive yet; it is simulated more simply.)
  • All RViz features are explained in Planning in RViz2 of the Operator PC documentation.

docs.title: Look at the numbers (optional)
docs.text:
In terminal 4, the joint positions the drives report, in radians:

cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe \
  bash -c 'ros2 topic echo --once /joint_states --field position'

After ready the values are close to 0, 0.5, 0.8, 0, 0.6 for j1_base … j5_wrist (the first value is the gripper).

docs.title: Part D: stop everything
docs.text:
1. In terminals 3 and 2: press Ctrl+C and wait until the prompt comes back.

  2. In any terminal:

    cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Operator-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml down
cd ~/smx/SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml down
docker stop dxl1 dxl2 dxl3 dxl4 dxl5 dxl6

Next time start again with Part B.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see Why What to do docker: command not found in Ubuntu Docker Desktop is not running, or its WSL integration is off Start Docker Desktop; step A2 wsl opens a window that closes at once, or errors about bash Windows opened the docker-desktop system instead of Ubuntu Open Ubuntu 24.04 from the Start menu, or once in PowerShell: wsl --set-default Ubuntu-24.04 Terminal 2 stays at waiting for the virtual bus … The drives do not run Step B1 in terminal 1 Terminal 2: no drive answers on ID n One drive kept an old ID docker stop dxl1 dxl2 dxl3 dxl4 dxl5 dxl6, then B1 and B2 again Terminal 3: network smx_net declared as external, but could not be found The Operator PC was started before the Robot PC Start the Robot PC first (B2) Terminal 3: could not connect to display :0 RViz cannot reach your screen Step A4; start terminal 3 from Ubuntu, not from PowerShell Address already in use An old container still holds its address Part D, then start again Plan & Execute ends with failed or the arm does not move The Robot PC is not up, or a goal out of reach Wait for gripper_controller in terminal 2; try the named goals ready and home Everything is very slow Little memory for Docker Close other programs; Docker Desktop Settings → Resources

docs.title: What you have just run
docs.text:
• The Operator PC and the Robot PC talked over ROS 2 on a Docker network, as they will over Wi-Fi on the real robot. Code you write for the Operator PC runs on the real arm later without changes.
  • The Robot PC used the same software it will use on the arm: ros2_control with the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL hardware interface.
  • The drives were the real doppelstep firmware, compiled as a Linux program with a simulated motor, joined into one bus by a small tool of the Robot PC.

This setup is called SIL (software in the loop). How it is built and how to judge its log in detail: Tutorial: checking SIL step by step. How the connections of the real robot will look: Connection guide for beginners.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text: SmartManipulator-X has three parts: the Operator PC plans motions, the Robot PC runs ROS 2 control and is the master of a DYNAMIXEL bus, and one doppelstep drive per stepper motor answers on that bus as a DYNAMIXEL servo. This page shows how they connect, who owns what, where the ROBOTIS software is reused, and in which operating modes the system runs.

docs.title: Project objective
docs.text:
The target is to use the ROS 2 control and operator-software concepts of ROBOTIS OpenMANIPULATOR-X with the mechanical design of BCN3D Moveo. Instead of DYNAMIXEL actuators, each stepper joint has a doppelstep drive that answers on a DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 bus as an XM430-W350 servo. The Robot PC, a Raspberry Pi CM4 on a CM4-Duino board, is the bus master and runs the unchanged ROBOTIS host software.

These sources have different roles. OpenMANIPULATOR-X is the reference for the ROS/DYNAMIXEL software stack; BCN3D Moveo is the mechanical reference. The OpenMANIPULATOR-X robot geometry, joints, actuator assumptions, and hardware configuration must not be copied as if they described Moveo.

What is implemented today is on the project status page.

docs.title: Software reuse boundary
docs.text:
The physical control path is:

MoveIt 2 (Operator PC)
  -> ROS 2 DDS
  -> ros2_control (Robot PC)
  -> ROBOTIS dynamixel_hardware_interface
  -> DynamixelSDK
  -> /dev/ttyDXL (CM4 PL011 UART0) -> half-duplex interface
  -> DYNAMIXEL bus: doppelstep IDs 1-6 (XM430-W350), gripper ID 7 (separate project)
  -> stepper motors / MG996R servo

Reuse the stock ROBOTIS hardware interface. doppelstep reports the real XM430-W350 model number (1020) and its Control Table, so no project-specific hardware interface and no custom model file are planned. What the Jazzy hardware interface actually reads and writes must still be checked against doppelstep in the compatibility specification before it is relied on.

The bus carries only DYNAMIXEL packets. Protocol 2.0 is already a collision-free master/slave protocol, so no second link layer is added; that keeps DynamixelSDK, DYNAMIXEL Wizard and USB-to-DYNAMIXEL adapters usable on the bus.

Reusing the OpenMANIPULATOR-X ROS application does not make its robot model or joint/controller configuration valid for Moveo. MoveIt planning groups, joint names, limits, kinematics, transmission assumptions, ros2_control interfaces, and controller configuration must agree with the Moveo description and the physical stepper setup.

The Robot PC image is intentionally separate from the Operator PC runtime. MoveIt, RViz2, and Gazebo do not belong in the Robot PC image.

docs.title: Operating assumptions
docs.text:
• The Robot PC software runs in Docker with ROS 2 Jazzy (Ubuntu 24.04 image); the host is Raspberry Pi OS on the CM4, or any Docker host during development.
  • Only the Robot PC owns the bus. The Operator PC never connects to the drives.
  • DDS domain ID, interface selection, discovery and firewall policy are configured consistently on both hosts. SSH is for administration, not the ROS data path.
  • Positioning is open loop: no encoders, no limit switches, no homing yet. The arm is placed in the start pose by hand before power-up.
  • Power-up order and an emergency stop are still open and must be defined before the full arm moves.

docs.title: DYNAMIXEL bus
docs.text:
The Robot PC drives the joints over one DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 bus. The CM4 is the bus master; the six doppelstep drives answer as XM430-W350 servos. The bus carries only standard DYNAMIXEL packets, so it is built for the ROBOTIS host software, DYNAMIXEL Wizard and a USB-to-DYNAMIXEL adapter without changes; the compatibility specification records what is verified.

Status (2026-11-15): decisions D4–D8 of the integration plan are agreed. The drives share one bus in SIL (SIL run 10); the wire itself is built and measured in Stages 2 and 3.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
CM4-Duino (bus master)
   GPIO14 TXD0 ─┐
   GPIO15 RXD0 ─┤ bus interface (open-drain send, echo-blocking receive)
                └── DATA ──┬───────────┬───────────┬── … ──┐
                    GND  ──┼───────────┼───────────┼── … ──┤
                           │           │           │       │
                       doppelstep  doppelstep  doppelstep  doppelstep
                         ID 1        ID 2        ID 3   …    ID 6

Only one device sends at a time: the master sends an instruction packet and only the addressed device answers with a status packet (Sync/Bulk Read answers come one after another in ID order). Protocol 2.0 needs no extra arbitration, so no second protocol layer is used on this bus (decision D4).

docs.title: Direction control on the master
docs.text:
The CM4 sends and receives on separate pins; the bus has one data line. The interface between them must release the line right after the last stop bit, before the addressed drive answers (Return Delay Time), and it must keep the CM4 from receiving its own packets, because DynamixelSDK does not discard an echo. Switching a direction GPIO from Linux user space is too slow and too jittery for this, so the interface needs no direction signal:

  • Send: an open-drain buffer (74LVC1G07) pulls DATA low for every 0 bit of TXD0; one pull-up resistor at the master pulls DATA high.
  • Receive: an OR gate passes DATA to RXD0 only while TXD0 is high, so the CM4's own 0 bits never reach its receiver.
  • Drives: the STM32 USART runs in single-wire half-duplex mode with its pin open-drain, so all devices only pull the line low.

Circuit, parts and pins: Wiring. It is built on a breadboard first (Stage 3) and may later become a shield for the CM4-Duino. If the noise measurements of Stage 4 require RS-485, an auto-direction transceiver replaces the open-drain stage at every node.

docs.title: Power and ground
docs.text:
Full wiring: Wiring.

  • Keep the bus cable short and away from the motor phases; measure the noise on the assembled arm before deciding between TTL and RS-485.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Each doppelstep drive is a DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 device that controls one stepper motor of the BCN3D Moveo. The Robot PC drives all of them through the stock ROBOTIS dynamixel_hardware_interface and DynamixelSDK. The gripper (ID 7) is a separate project and gets its own rows when it starts.

The ROBOTIS OpenMANIPULATOR-X source is a software-stack reference, not evidence that its stock actuator model, joint names, motion ranges, or register usage fit the Moveo build.

docs.title: Verification record
docs.text:
For each test, record hardware and firmware revisions, host OS/ROS distribution, exact source commits, configuration, command, expected result, and observed result. Distinguish the simulated drive (native_sim) from a physical stepper axis.

Minimum staged evidence:

  1. SIL: the Robot PC opens the virtual bus and pings every simulated drive (Stage 1).
  2. Verify Protocol 2.0 framing and status/error responses against the selected DynamixelSDK transport.
  3. Record the read/write transactions of the hardware-interface start-up and update loop and check each against doppelstep.
  4. Bench: one B-G431B-ESC1 over the ST-LINK virtual COM port follows trajectories from the Operator PC (Stage 2).
  5. Single-wire physical layer: the same tests through the half-duplex interface at the chosen baud rate.
  6. One physical joint on the arm with its scaling, limits, reference method and stop behavior (Stage 4).

docs.title: SIL run 1 (2026-11-15)
docs.text:
Robot PC image built from this repository (ROBOTIS jazzy branches), six doppelstep native_sim drives (firmware 52, model 1020) in Docker, tools/sim/smx_dxl_bus.py, hardware:=sil.

Observed Result Port, baud change on the pseudo-terminal OK PING of IDs 1–6, model 1020 → xm430_w350.model OK Torque state read, Operating Mode 4, Return Delay Time 0, Drive Mode 0 / 1 (ID 3) written OK Read path: Fast Sync Read through indirect addresses (address 634, 10 bytes: Present Position, Velocity, Current) Set up OK; first readings wrong (j2 206080 rad, j4 3.3·10⁶ rad) Write path: Sync Write through indirect addresses (address 224, 4 bytes: Goal Position) Set up OK Torque Enable write at activation Crash: stack smashing detected in DynamixelSDK Protocol2PacketHandler::writeTxRx error_timeout_sec Not a parameter of the interface; the name is error_timeout_ms (default 500 ms)

Cause: the first version of the virtual bus did not pass a drive's bytes to the other drives. Fast Sync Read needs that (the drives append their parts to one common status packet in turn), so the host received a malformed answer; a stray long status packet then reached writeTxRx, which reads the status into an 11-byte buffer on the stack. Fixed in the bus (drive-to-drive forwarding, test test_other_drives_hear_the_answer) and in the xacro (error_timeout_ms). Note for the real bus: a malformed or late long status packet can crash the host process in DynamixelSDK; bus noise must not produce one silently.

docs.title: SIL run 2 (2026-11-15)
docs.text:
Same setup with drive-to-drive forwarding in the bus. Same result: wrong positions (j2 −718751 rad, j4 2.2·10⁶ rad), then the crash at Torque Enable.

Cause, from the source of dynamixel_hardware_interface (5613760, 2026-11-02) and the doppelstep documentation:

  • The interface always tries Fast Sync Read first (use_fast_read_protocol_ is hard-coded true, no hardware parameter). It falls back to normal Sync Read only if the first 10 Fast Sync Read attempts fail; after one success it keeps Fast Sync Read for good.
  • doppelstep answers Fast Sync/Bulk Read only for its own ID (DYNAMIXEL emulation): with six drives the host gets six packets instead of one chained packet, accepts the first as a success and decodes the rest as garbage.

This also applies to the real bus with six doppelstep drives. Options: (a) doppelstep chains Fast Sync/Bulk Read answers like the X series (listens to the drive before it), or (b) doppelstep stays silent on a Fast Sync/Bulk Read that lists other IDs too, so the host falls back to Sync Read. Tracked in Stage 0 of the integration plan.

SIL workaround until run 10: the virtual bus dropped Fast Sync/Bulk Read (--fast-read drop), which is the behaviour of option (b). Since run 10 the drives implement option (b) themselves.

docs.title: SIL run 3 (2026-11-15)
docs.text:
With Fast Sync Read dropped by the bus, the interface fell back to Sync Read as designed, but every Sync Read of IDs 1–6 ended in COMM_RX_TIMEOUT (−3001) and the activation stopped after 500 ms (Dynamixel Start Fail … SYNC_READ_FAIL). No crash.

Measured with tools/sim/smx_bus_timing.py on the virtual bus: PING 3–17 ms per drive (the 10 ms polling of the doppelstep pseudo-terminal); a Sync Read of six IDs gets all six answers within 13–21 ms, below the DynamixelSDK timeout (35 ms at 1 Mbps), but in random order, for example ID 2, 1, 5, 3, 4, 6. DynamixelSDK reads the answers in the order of the request and drops an answer with another ID, so the later IDs time out.

This also applies to the real bus: each doppelstep answers a Sync Read (and Bulk Read) at once instead of waiting for its turn, so on one wire the answers of six drives would collide. The X series answers in the order of the request (a device sends after the status packet of the ID before it). Tracked in Stage 0 of the integration plan.

SIL workaround until run 10: the virtual bus passed Sync/Bulk Read answers to the host in request order (--read-order request). Since run 10 the drives take turns themselves.

docs.title: SIL run 4 (2026-11-15): pass
docs.text:
Virtual bus with Fast Sync Read dropped and Sync Read answers in request order. Fast Sync Read fails 10 times, the interface switches to Sync Read, reads plausible positions, enables torque on IDs 1–6 and activates; joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller become active. smx_smoke_test.sh from a second container: PASS (trajectory executed by the six simulated doppelstep drives).

Timing in SIL run 4: each Sync Read took 10–20 ms (10 ms polling of the simulated drives), so the 100 Hz controller loop overran in most cycles, and about 2–3 Sync Reads per second timed out. SIL was then changed to 50 Hz and baud_rate 9600 (run 7); run 8 found the real cause of the timeouts and moved SIL to 25 Hz. Simulation-only: on a real bus an answer takes well under 1 ms.

docs.title: SIL run 7 (2026-11-15)
docs.text: 50 Hz, baud_rate 9600, error timeout 5 s, reorder timeout of the bus 100 ms. Start and fallback to Sync Read as in run 4. In about 35 s: 82 SyncRead Rx Fail (about 2.3 per second, each recovered in the next cycle) and 31 overruns. A normal Sync Read takes about 20–21 ms, the whole 50 Hz cycle, and a failed cycle ends after about 21 ms as well: the host gives up after about 20 ms whatever the baud rate, so the expected longer DynamixelSDK packet timeout at 9600 is not in effect. Open: the bus now logs each incomplete read (missing ID, delay of every answer) and a latency summary every 10 s; the next run is to show whether one drive is late or the timeout of the host is fixed.

docs.title: SIL run 8 (2026-11-15): pass, no read timeouts
docs.text:
Same setup as run 7. The bus diagnostics answered the open question: no read was incomplete (all six answers arrived every time; last answer after p50 12.7 / p95 21 / max 25.6 ms), yet the host reported 96 SyncRead Rx Fail (−3001, COMM_RX_TIMEOUT) and 24 overruns in about 30 s. Cause: in the control loop dynamixel_hardware_interface sets the packet timeout to the control period, port_handler->setPacketTimeout(period_ms) in Dynamixel::ProcessReadCommunication, which replaces the timeout DynamixelSDK derives from the baud rate. At 50 Hz the host gives up after 20 ms, and every Sync Read whose last answer comes later fails. This is why changing the baud rate had no effect.

Fix: SIL runs the controllers at 25 Hz (SMX_UPDATE_RATE, period 40 ms). Result: smx_smoke_test.sh PASS, 0 SyncRead Rx Fail and 0 overruns after start; the only read errors are the ten expected Fast Sync Read attempts before the fallback.

For the real bus: the read timeout of the host is one control period (10 ms at 100 Hz), not the DynamixelSDK timeout. A Sync Read of all drives, including their return delay times, must therefore finish well within one period.

docs.title: SIL run 9 (2026-11-15): MoveIt from the Operator PC
docs.text:
Same setup as run 8, with the Operator PC (move_group, RViz2) on smx_net. Two MoveGroup goals (plan and execute) to the SRDF poses ready (0, 0.5, 0.8, 0, 0.6 rad) and home (all 0): both SUCCEEDED, Completed trajectory execution with status SUCCEEDED in move_group, no SyncRead Rx Fail, no overrun, no incomplete read on the bus. This meets the exit of Stage 1.

Observed: after each motion the joints stand 5–6 encoder steps (0.008–0.011 rad) from the goal, for example j2_shoulder 0.492 instead of 0.5. Within the 0.01 rad tolerance of the goal; not investigated yet whether the cause is the simulated drive (position loop, step resolution) or the trajectory controller.

docs.title: SIL run 10 (2026-11-15): pass, the drives handle the shared bus
docs.text:
Stage 0 in the firmware: X430 emulator 1.1.0 in doppelstep. A drive answers a Sync Read or Bulk Read only after it has received the status packet of the ID listed before it, and stays silent on a Fast Sync/Bulk Read that lists other IDs too (options of runs 2 and 3). The virtual bus now behaves like the wire: it passes Fast Sync Read on and the answers in the order they arrive (--fast-read forward --read-order arrival, its new default).

Observed (about 12 min, Operator PC with MoveIt on smx_net) Result Fast Sync Read at start Reaches the drives; they stay silent, 10 failed attempts, then Sync Read Sync Read of IDs 1–6 7,364 reads, 0 incomplete, 0 SyncRead Rx Fail, 0 overruns at 10 Hz Time to the last answer of a read p50 44 / p95 61 / max 65 ms: six drives one after the other smx_smoke_test.sh, two MoveIt goals (ready, home) PASS, SUCCEEDED

At 25 Hz the same setup gave 85 SyncRead Rx Fail in about 30 s: Zephyr native_sim emulates the UART interrupt of a drive with a thread that wakes every 10 ms (fixed in uart_native_pty.c), so each turn costs up to 10 ms. SIL therefore runs at 10 Hz. On the board the UART interrupt is immediate.

Robot description of the controller manager. In this run the Robot PC first loaded mock hardware for hardware:=sil: the Operator PC was started first, and MoveIt published its own /robot_description (with mock hardware) on the shared DDS domain. The controller manager takes the first description it receives, and the remapping of ~/robot_description in robot.launch.py had no effect (ros2_control 4.48 subscribes to robot_description). Fixed on both sides: the controller manager reads a topic that only the Robot PC publishes (/smx/robot_pc/control_description), and MoveIt no longer publishes /robot_description. Check with ros2 control list_hardware_components: in SIL the arm is dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware.

How to repeat the check: SIL tutorial.

Do not claim full XM430 emulation or production readiness based only on successful packet exchange. Register behavior, mechanical mapping, and physical motion all require separate evidence.

docs.title: doppelstep joint drives
docs.text:
Each stepper joint of the arm is driven by its own doppelstep drive: a small stepper controller that answers on the DYNAMIXEL bus as a smart servo. For the Robot PC every joint motor therefore looks like a DYNAMIXEL XM430-W350, so the unchanged ROBOTIS dynamixel_hardware_interface and DynamixelSDK are meant to drive it (to be verified, see the compatibility specification).

Status (2026-11-15): doppelstep v0.3.0 (2026-11-14) is verified on a PC with a simulated motor (native_sim) and on a B-G431B-ESC1 with a real motor (17HS19-2004S1 at 12 V and 24 V: the test scenarios of the bench GUI, the protection comparators, two minutes of moves at 1.5 A, the wiring self-test, the measured dead time; DYNAMIXEL Wizard 2.0 over the ST-LINK virtual COM port). Not yet with the motors and loads of the arm, and not yet on a shared bus with the Robot PC (Stage 2). The single-wire bus is built (single-wire.overlay) and several drives share a bus in SIL; on a board it is tested in Stage 2. The doppelstep documentation is authoritative for the drive; this page records only what SmartManipulator-X relies on and links to the details.

docs.title: Gripper servo (MG996R)
docs.text:
The gripper is driven by an MG996R hobby servo. On the bus it will appear as a virtual DYNAMIXEL device on ID 7, so gripper_controller and the joint contract stay unchanged.

Status (2026-11-15): separate project, not started. It begins after the chain Operator PC → Robot PC → doppelstep works (decision D9 of the integration plan). Until then the gripper runs on mock hardware. The MCU of the gripper node is open.

Sources: Handsontec MG996R Metal Gear Servo Motor user guide (MG996R.pdf on the manufacturer's website, link checked on 2026-11-15). If the link stops working, the repository keeps a backup copy (docs/hardware/datasheets/Handsontec_MG996R_user_guide.pdf, not published on this website).

docs.title: Datasheet values
docs.text:
Parameter Value (Handsontec user guide) Operating voltage 4.8–7.2 V Stall torque 9.4 kgf·cm at 4.8 V, 11 kgf·cm at 6 V Operating speed 0.17 s/60° at 4.8 V, 0.14 s/60° at 6 V Running current 500 mA Stall current 2.5 A at 6 V Dead band width 5 µs Control signal PWM, 20 ms period (50 Hz), 1–2 ms pulse Positions ~1 ms = one end, 1.5 ms = middle, ~2 ms = other end Rotation approximately 120° for 1–2 ms Weight, dimensions 55 g; 40.7 × 19.7 × 42.9 mm Connector 3-pin, brown = ground (−), red = +V, orange = signal

Shop listings often say "180°" and "13 kg·cm"; plan with the datasheet values and measure the real angle per millisecond on the gripper (see Calibration).

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text: Gripper servo wiring: the gripper node on the bus drives the orange signal wire; the servo gets +6 V from its own converter; grounds meet at the star point Servo wire Connects to Notes Orange (signal) PWM output of the gripper node, 3.3 V logic, 50 Hz Short wire, routed with the ground Red (+V) +6 V of the servo DC/DC converter Never from a logic supply: the servo draws up to 2.5 A Brown (−) Minus of the servo DC/DC converter and the GND star point The servo current must not flow through the bus ground Item Specification Converter DC/DC from V_M to 6 V, ≥ 5 A, for the servo only; stay within 4.8–7.2 V Bulk capacitor Low-ESR electrolytic, 470–1000 µF, ≥ 10 V, at the servo connector, against dips at start and stall (project practice, not from the datasheet) Wires +6 V and − at least 0.5 mm² Gripper node DATA and GND from the DYNAMIXEL bus, its own logic supply (open, part of the gripper project)

docs.title: Signal level
docs.text: The gripper node drives a 3.3 V signal. Most MG996R servos switch reliably at 3.3 V, but the datasheet gives no input threshold. If the servo jitters although the pulses are clean on an oscilloscope, add a one-way level shifter such as a 74AHCT125 powered from 5 V. Never pull the signal up to the 6 V servo supply: that would drive more than 3.3 V into the MCU pin.

docs.title: Behavior the gripper node must provide
docs.text: Topic Requirement Protocol DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 device on ID 7, same bus parameters as the drives Pulse 50 Hz, 1000–2000 µs, ≥ 1 µs resolution (servo dead band 5 µs) Torque off No pulses: the servo is limp Start The servo position after power-up is unknown; the first Torque ON moves at full speed to the start position Speed Software ramp of the pulse width (Profile Velocity), because the servo itself always moves at full speed Limits Position limits stored in the device, set from the calibration

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The servo has no position feedback. Find the end positions by hand:

  1. Low profile velocity, Torque ON.
  2. Move in steps of 1–2° towards closed until the jaws just touch, then back off by 2–3°. Note the angle. Do not hold the servo against a stop: it then draws the stall current of 2.5 A and heats up.
  3. Do the same towards open.
  4. Store both values as position limits.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
1. Plug or unplug the servo only with the 6 V converter off.
  2. Only 3.3 V signals from the gripper node; no pull-up to the servo supply.
  3. Torque OFF removes the pulses: the gripper may open under load.
  4. Keep hands out of the gripper at the first Torque ON after power-up.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
How the Robot PC board, the joint drives, the gripper servo and the supplies are connected. The DYNAMIXEL bus page explains the bus itself; this page is the wiring reference to build from. New to electronics? Start with the connection guide for beginners.

Status (2026-11-15): proposed wiring, nothing is built yet. Pins of the CM4-Duino come from the Waveshare documentation, the drive connectors from the ST B-G431B-ESC1 schematic (MB1419 rev. C-01), and the motor and supply data from the doppelstep Hardware and bring-up page, which is authoritative for the drive. Items marked to confirm must be checked before power is applied.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Power distribution: motor PSU through the emergency stop and the main fuse to six drives and the servo converter; separate 5 V supply for the CM4-Duino; one ground star point DYNAMIXEL bus: the CM4-Duino and the bus interface feed DATA and GND in a daisy chain to drives 1–6 and the gripper node Rule Why One ground star point at the minus terminal of the motor PSU Motor currents must not flow through the bus ground or the CM4-Duino The CM4-Duino has its own 5 V supply and reaches ground only through the bus GND No ground loop through two supplies Bus DATA and GND twisted together, away from the motor phase wires The stepper phases switch at 20 kHz with steep edges Plug or unplug motors, servo and bus only with all supplies off Hot-plugging a stepper can destroy the power stage; the bus pins are not protected

docs.title: Robot PC: CM4-Duino to the bus interface
docs.text:
Bus interface: GPIO14 TXD0 drives DATA through an open-drain buffer; DATA returns to GPIO15 RXD0 through an OR gate that blocks the echo CM4-Duino pin Signal Interface D14 (GPIO14, TXD0) UART transmit U1 input A, U2 input A D15 (GPIO15, RXD0) UART receive U3 output Y 3V3 (power header) 3.3 V supply of the interface and the pull-up U1–U3 VCC, R1 GND Ground U1–U3 GND, BUS pin 2 Part Value Function U1 74LVC1G07 Open-drain buffer: pulls DATA low while TXD0 is low U2 74LVC1G04 Inverter: /TX U3 74LVC1G32 OR of DATA and /TX: RXD0 follows DATA only while TXD0 is high, so the CM4 does not receive its own packets R1 470 Ω to 3V3 Bus pull-up, the only one on the bus; sized for about 1.5 m of cable at 1 Mbps R2, C1 100 Ω, 100 pF Delay DATA by about 10 ns against /TX, so no glitch reaches RXD0 at a falling edge C 100 nF per IC Decoupling

The drives configure their bus pin as open-drain in half-duplex mode, so all devices only pull DATA low and R1 pulls it high: no device can drive against another. To confirm in Stage 3: rise time on the full cable at 1 Mbps (R1 may need to go down to 330 Ω), and that the OR gate really suppresses the echo (dynamixel_sdk ping with a logic analyzer on TXD0, DATA and RXD0).

Why not a direction GPIO: switching a GPIO from Linux after the last stop bit is too slow and too jittery for the Return Delay Time of the drives. The circuit above needs no direction signal at all.

docs.title: Joint drives: B-G431B-ESC1
docs.text: One doppelstep drive: motor supply on J5/J6, stepper coils on J7, bus on J3 pin 2 (PB3) and pin 5 (GND)

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
Connector Pin Net (schematic) Connect to J5 + V+ Motor supply V_M (+) J6 − GND Motor supply ground J7 OUT1 Leg U (TIM1_CH1/CH1N, PA8/PC13) Motor A+ J7 OUT2 Leg V (TIM1_CH2/CH2N, PA9/PA12) Motor B+ J7 OUT3 Leg W (TIM1_CH3/CH3N, PA10/PB15), shared Motor A− and B− J3 1 +5V (output of the on-board 5 V regulator) Not connected J3 2 USART2_TX, PB3 Bus DATA J3 3 USART2_RX, PB4 Not connected (half-duplex uses PB3 only) J3 4 PWM, PA15 Not connected J3 5 GND Bus GND ST-LINK USB – ST-LINK/V2-1 on the detachable part of the board Bench PC only: VCP (USART2 = the DYNAMIXEL bus), SWD flashing, RTT log

Notes:

  • J3, J5, J6 and J7 are solder pads on the board. Solder a 5-pin header to J3 and wires of sufficient cross-section to J5/J6/J7.
  • USART2 on PB3/PB4 is also the ST-LINK virtual COM port (through 0 Ω resistors R23/R24 on the ST-LINK part of the board). That is why the bench link of Stage 2 and the bus of the arm use the same UART. On the arm, leave the ST-LINK USB unplugged.
  • Motor coils: doppelstep uses a shared-leg topology, each coil between its own leg (U or V) and the common leg W (motor wiring). Leg W carries the sum of both coil currents, up to √2 times the phase current: use the same wire cross-section as for the supply. Before torque is enabled, doppelstep tests each coil and refuses torque if a coil is open, shorted or miswired.
  • Motor supply 24 V: the doppelstep firmware accepts 10–28 V and is tuned for 24 V (supply and bus voltage). The board input also has a TVS diode SMM4F26A (26 V stand-off) across V+, so do not go above 24 V nominal. First runs on a laboratory supply at 12 V with a current limit.
  • Before the first motor is connected, run the doppelstep bring-up checklist: dead time measured first, then offsets, current polarity, current loop, motion, protection.
  • Per-drive settings (ID, baud rate, direction) are listed on the doppelstep drives page.

docs.title: Joint motors
docs.text:
ID Joint Motor Rated current Notes 1 j1_base NEMA 17, 17HS19-2504S 2.5 A 2 j2_shoulder (a) NEMA 23, 23HS2430 3.0 A 3 j2_shoulder (b) NEMA 23, 23HS2430 3.0 A Faces motor (a): runs mirrored (Drive Mode reverse) 4 j3_elbow NEMA 17, 17HS19-1684S-PG5 1.68 A Planetary gearbox 5.18:1 (57/11), at most 2 N·m at the output 5 j4_forearm_roll NEMA 17, 17HS13-0404S1 0.4 A Never run it with the current setting of a larger motor 6 j5_wrist NEMA 14, 14HS20-1504S 1.5 A

Set the run current of every drive to the rated current of its motor before the first move (doppelstep configuration). Wire colors differ between the motor types and batches; identify the two coils with an ohmmeter (a few ohms within a coil, open between coils) instead of trusting colors. A swapped coil end only reverses the current sign; step 3 of the doppelstep bring-up checklist detects it.

docs.title: Gripper servo
docs.text: The gripper is a separate project; its wiring is on the gripper servo page.

docs.title: Power-up order and checks
docs.text:
1. All supplies off. Check with a multimeter: no short between V_M and GND at each drive; no connection between bus DATA and V_M.
  2. CM4-Duino on (5 V USB-C). Check DATA idles at 3.3 V.
  3. Motor supply on (E-stop released). Drives start with torque off; a supply below 10 V or above 28 V trips the doppelstep protection.
  4. Ping every ID from the Robot PC before enabling torque.

Power-down in reverse order. An emergency stop that cuts V_M is planned and must exist before the full arm moves (project status).

docs.title: CM4-Duino Robot PC board
docs.text:
The Robot PC of SmartManipulator-X runs on a Waveshare CM4-Duino carrier board with a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 (variant with Wi-Fi). The board has the size and header layout of an Arduino Uno R3 and exposes the CM4 GPIO, an 8-channel ADC, HDMI, one USB 2.0 port, a camera connector and an M.2 slot.

Why this page is so detailed: the CM4-Duino is no longer sold through the official Waveshare channels and its wiki page may disappear. This page keeps everything the project needs from the Waveshare wiki, retrieved on 2026-11-15; the links below point to the vendor files on the Waveshare servers. If this page and the schematic disagree, the schematic is authoritative; update this page.

Status (2026-11-15): board selected, not yet brought up in this project. Nothing below is verified on our hardware unless marked so.

Waveshare drawings: pinout (Arduino-style headers with the CM4 GPIO numbers and functions) and onboard components.

docs.title: Software setup
docs.text: The paths below are for Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (/boot/firmware/config.txt; Bullseye and older use /boot/config.txt).

docs.title: Flashing the eMMC
docs.text:
1. Set the BOOT switch to ON and connect the Type-C port to a PC. Connect nothing else, so the CM4 is powered only from the PC.
  2. Run rpiboot on the PC (Raspberry Pi usbboot; Waveshare ships a Windows installer, Rpiboot_setup.zip). The eMMC appears as a USB drive.
  3. Write the image with Raspberry Pi Imager.
  4. Set the BOOT switch to OFF, power the board from a 5 V / 3 A supply.

A CM4 Lite boots from the microSD card instead; prepare the card on a PC.

docs.title: USB 2.0 port
docs.text:
The port is off by default to save power. Enable it in config.txt:

dtoverlay=dwc2,dr_mode=host

Raspberry Pi OS images after 2021-10-30 set otg_mode=1 in the [cm4] section. The port then still works but the kernel logs config failed, hub doesn't have any ports! (err -19). Remove otg_mode=1 and keep the dtoverlay line above to get rid of it.

docs.title: ADC (ADS7830)
docs.text:
• I²C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3), address 0x48 by default; enable I²C in raspi-config or with dtparam=i2c_arm=on.
  • Single-ended inputs by default (differential possible), 8 bit, reference on AD_REF.
  • An unconnected input reads random values.
  • Waveshare's Python example is archived as CM4-duino-code.zip (ADS7830.py, run with sudo python3 ADS7830.py).

docs.title: Camera
docs.text: Not used by the project now; kept for completeness. Only CAM0 exists. Add the overlay of the sensor to config.txt, for example dtoverlay=imx219,cam0 (others: ov5647, ov9281, imx290 with clock-frequency=37125000, imx296, imx378, imx477, imx519, imx708), reboot and test with libcamera-hello --list-cameras. If the log says Camera frontend has timed out!, update the firmware (sudo rpi-update).

docs.title: Settings used by this project
docs.text:
Planned, see Robot PC on the CM4-Duino:

# /boot/firmware/config.txt  (SmartManipulator-X, planned)
enable_uart=1
dtoverlay=disable-bt          # PL011 UART0 on GPIO14/15 for the DYNAMIXEL bus
dtoverlay=dwc2,dr_mode=host   # USB 2.0 port (only if a USB device is needed)

  • Use a 5 V / 3 A supply on Type-C; the motor supply of the arm stays separate (see DYNAMIXEL bus).
