docs.title: BCN3D Moveo mechanics
docs.text: The arm is a BCN3D Moveo. This page says where the mechanical design comes from, how the ROS model is generated from its CAD, which conventions the model uses, and what is still to be measured on the assembled arm.

docs.title: Mechanical source
docs.text:
The target arm mechanics are based on the BCN3D Moveo project, not on the OpenMANIPULATOR-X geometry. The upstream repository provides CAD files, STL files, assembly/user documentation, a bill of materials, and original firmware. Its README describes an educational, additively manufactured arm controlled by Arduino-based electronics.

This project replaces/adapts the control electronics; it does not claim that the original Moveo firmware or electronics are part of the SmartManipulator-X control path. Refer to the upstream repository and its license for the authoritative mechanical files, assembly details, and attribution requirements.

docs.title: ROS model integration
docs.text:
The project-owned ROS model is in:

ros2_ws/src/smartmanipulator_x/smartmanipulator_x_description/

The model in that package is generated from the BCN3D Moveo CAD: a STEP export of BCN3D Moveo assembly.SLDASM (upstream CAD files/, MIT license; the license text is in meshes/LICENSE-BCN3D-Moveo). The scripts in tools/cad/ read the STEP, assign each part to a link, take the joint axes from the axles in the CAD, and write urdf/smartmanipulator_x.urdf.xacro, the decimated visual meshes, and convex-hull collision meshes. See tools/cad/README.md for the steps; meshes/geometry.json records the derived values.

Quantity From the CAD Base (table plate top) to J2 axis 231.64 mm J2 to J3 221.12 mm J3 to J5, along the J4 roll axis 223.00 mm (J4 joint frame at 96.09 mm, where the wrist part begins) Gripper MG996R servo gear and idler gear with 40 mm arms, pivot arms of the same length: a parallelogram; 80 mm finger gap when open

Conventions of the model:

  • Zero pose: arm straight up, gripper fully open. The start pose (arm placed by hand before power-up) must match it, or the zero offsets must be set in the drives (Homing Offset).
  • Positive J2, J3 and J5 bend the arm forward (+x, away from the electronics box of the original Moveo); positive J1 and J4 turn counter-clockwise seen from the tip of their axis.
  • gripper is the servo gear angle, 0 (open) to 1.45 rad (closed). The idler gear, pivot arms and fingers are mimic joints.
  • The original electronics box is available with the xacro argument electronics_box:=true; it is off by default because this build uses other electronics.

Still to verify on the assembled arm: joint limits (the URDF values are placeholders), the direction of each motor against the conventions above, and any printed part changed for the NEMA 23 shoulder or the geared elbow motor.

When integrating the model:

  • Use BCN3D Moveo geometry and assembly as the mechanical source of truth.
  • Record the source revision and any project-specific changes to CAD/STL-derived geometry.
  • Establish the base frame, link frames, joint axes, zero positions, and units from the source design and assembled robot.
  • Verify joint ranges and collision geometry against the physical arm; do not inherit OpenMANIPULATOR-X limits or joint names.
  • Define and document each Moveo joint-to-stepper mapping, transmission, microstepping, homing/reference method, and position scaling once they are measured on the assembled arm (the motors are listed in Joint motors).
  • Keep MoveIt planning groups, ros2_control joints, Gazebo joints, and physical motor mapping consistent.
  • Preserve upstream license and attribution notices for imported or adapted assets. Do not assume that the project repository's license changes third-party asset licensing.

The electronics are described in Wiring: one doppelstep drive per stepper motor, with the motor of each joint listed in Joint motors (J1 base, J2 shoulder with two motors, J3 elbow, J4 forearm roll, J5 wrist), plus an MG996R gripper servo. Joint limits, motor directions and gear ratios are still to be measured on the assembled arm; there are no encoders or limit switches yet, so the start pose is set by hand.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text: Before a model is treated as the canonical robot description, validate that it parses in URDF/Xacro tooling, has a connected link tree and correct joint types/axes, and produces a useful RViz visualization. Compare each joint range and frame placement with the assembled Moveo. Then check that the same joint contract can be loaded by both the physical ros2_control configuration and the selected Gazebo integration.

docs.title: Operator PC
docs.text: The Operator PC is the computer the operator works on: it plans and visualizes motions and talks to the Robot PC over ROS 2 DDS. Its software lives in a separate repository; this page describes its role and what it must agree on with the Robot PC.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
The Operator PC owns motion planning, operator visualization, and simulation workflows:

  • MoveIt 2 planning and execution clients.
  • RViz2 visualization and operator-facing configuration.
  • Gazebo simulation and simulation-specific ros2_control integration.
  • ROS 2 DDS communication with the Robot PC over the configured network.

It does not own the DYNAMIXEL bus, the doppelstep drives, or the physical ros2_control hardware interface. Do not pass any serial device through to the Operator PC.

docs.title: Separate repository
docs.text:
Operator PC implementation is maintained in the separate sfs-smartmanipulator-x-operator repository; this documentation contains its architecture guidance only. Keep Operator-specific launch files, MoveIt configuration, RViz setup, Gazebo assets, and runtime/container configuration in that repository. The Robot PC Docker image must remain free of Operator PC GUI and simulation dependencies.

Consume the canonical robot description from smartmanipulator_x_description (in the Robot PC repository) or a future shared-description repository. The package is generated from the BCN3D Moveo CAD (see BCN3D Moveo mechanics); its joint limits are placeholders until measured on the arm, so planning limits must be revisited then. Do not duplicate an independent URDF/Xacro or substitute the OpenMANIPULATOR-X model for Moveo.

docs.title: Real robot and simulation
docs.text:
The intended MoveIt application should work with either the physical Robot PC or simulation. The robot model, joint names, limits, planning groups, and controller-facing joint semantics must agree in both modes:

Real robot: MoveIt -> DDS -> Robot PC ros2_control -> DYNAMIXEL bus -> doppelstep drives
Simulation: MoveIt -> Gazebo ros2_control integration -> simulated Moveo joints

Use the physical path only after doppelstep compatibility and robot bring-up are verified. Gazebo integration and MoveIt configuration belong to the Operator PC repository.

docs.title: DDS checklist
docs.text: On the robot the Robot PC is reached over Wi-Fi (the CM4-Duino has no Ethernet connector). For two-host operation, configure matching ROS 2 domain IDs and verify that both hosts use reachable network interfaces. Check DDS discovery, routing/multicast support, and firewall rules in the deployment network. SSH can be used for administration, but it is not a substitute for DDS connectivity. Simulation-only runs can be local to the Operator PC and do not require physical hardware.

docs.title: Plan: doppelstep drives on a CM4-Duino Robot PC
docs.text: Status (2026-11-15): plan agreed, no implementation yet. This page defines the target architecture of the project. Update the checklists here as the work progresses; the summary is on the project status page.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Run the Robot PC software from this repository on a Waveshare CM4-Duino with a Raspberry Pi CM4 (with Wi-Fi). It drives the arm joints through sfs-doppelstep stepper drives that present themselves as DYNAMIXEL XM430-W350 servos (Protocol 2.0). The Operator PC (sfs-smartmanipulator-x-operator) stays unchanged and connects over ROS 2 DDS.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: # Decision Status D1 Joint drives: one doppelstep drive (ST B-G431B-ESC1) per stepper motor Agreed D2 One repository. This repo stays the Robot PC and builds the CM4 artifact (arm64 image + deployment files). No separate controller repo for the software. A separate repo only for a future interface PCB (KiCad) Agreed D3 Operator PC ↔ Robot PC link: Wi-Fi of the CM4 (the CM4-Duino has no RJ45 and only one USB 2.0 port) Agreed D4 Joint bus speaks plain DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0, with no second link layer: DXL is already a collision-free master/slave protocol, and a second MAC would break direct compatibility with DynamixelSDK, dynamixel_hardware_interface and DYNAMIXEL Wizard Agreed D5 Half-duplex single-wire UART driver is implemented in doppelstep (Zephyr, STM32G431 USART single-wire mode) Agreed D6 Bench link PC ↔ B-G431B-ESC1: ST-LINK VCP (keeps SWD/RTT debugging available). A separate USB-UART adapter only if needed later Agreed D7 Physical layer in the arm: TTL single-wire first; RS-485 (auto-direction transceiver) only if Stage 4 noise measurements require it. No real ROBOTIS servos share the bus, so the choice is free Agreed (2026-11-15) D8 Baud rate 1 Mbps (OpenMANIPULATOR-X default); doppelstep factory setting 57600, up to 4.5 Mbps; each drive is set once with tools/diagnostics/smx_drive_setup.py Agreed (2026-11-15); the ST-LINK VCP limit is checked in Stage 2 for the bench only D9 Gripper (MG996R, PWM): virtual DYNAMIXEL on ID 7 (small MCU reusing the doppelstep X430 emulator, PWM output), so the joint contract and gripper_controller stay unchanged. Built as a separate project after the chain Operator PC → Robot PC → doppelstep works; until then the gripper stays on mock hardware Agreed D10 Motor supply 24 V (doppelstep accepts 10–28 V and is tuned for 24 V; board TVS 26 V stand-off). First runs at 12 V on a laboratory supply with current limit Agreed (2026-11-15)

docs.title: Target architecture
docs.text:
Operator PC (MoveIt 2, RViz2)
        │  ROS 2 DDS over Wi-Fi (ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42)
        ▼
 CM4-Duino + CM4 (Raspberry Pi OS, Docker)
   robot_pc container (arm64): ros2_control
     -> dynamixel_hardware_interface -> DynamixelSDK
     -> /dev/ttyDXL (PL011 UART, GPIO14/15 on the Arduino header, BT disabled)
        │  DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0, half-duplex single-wire TTL, 1 Mbps
        ├── doppelstep ID 1  j1_base
        ├── doppelstep ID 2  j2_shoulder (motor A)
        ├── doppelstep ID 3  j2_shoulder (motor B, mirrored)
        ├── doppelstep ID 4  j3_elbow
        ├── doppelstep ID 5  j4_forearm_roll
        └── doppelstep ID 6  j5_wrist
   gripper MG996R: ID 7 virtual DXL (separate project, later)

The ID map is the existing joint contract; only the device behind each ID changes.

docs.title: Stage 0: bus decisions and half-duplex driver (doppelstep)
docs.text:
• Single-wire half-duplex USART in doppelstep: app/single-wire.overlay (single-wire; on &usart2, PB3 open-drain, MCUboot unchanged), built and checked in doppelstep CI. The test on a board (turnaround vs. Return Delay Time) needs a half-duplex USB adapter and moves to Stage 2
  • D7, D8 and D10 agreed (2026-11-15) and recorded in the compatibility specification
  • Fast Sync/Bulk Read with several drives (found in SIL, run 2): a drive stays silent when the request lists other IDs, the ROBOTIS interface falls back to Sync Read (X430 emulator 1.1.0, SIL run 10)
  • Sync Read / Bulk Read turn-taking (found in SIL, run 3): each drive answers after the status packet of the ID before it, and stays silent if it does not come within 100 ms (X430 emulator 1.1.0, SIL run 10)
  • IDs 1–6 and 1 Mbps on each drive: tools/diagnostics/smx_drive_setup.py writes ID and Baud Rate over the bus, one drive at a time (checked on a native_sim drive; on the real drives in Stage 2 and 4)
  • Secondary (Shadow) ID: supported by the X430 emulator, but dynamixel_hardware_interface addresses each ID itself; the mirrored J2 pair stays on transmission_to_joint_matrix (verified in SIL)

Exit: reached in SIL (run 10): six drives share the virtual bus without help from it; D7, D8 and D10 recorded. The single-wire wire itself is tested on the board in Stage 2.

docs.title: Stage 1: SIL on the PC, no hardware
docs.text:
• Virtual DXL bus tools/sim/smx_dxl_bus.py: connects N doppelstep native_sim instances over TCP into one half-duplex bus at /dev/ttyDXL (pty), assigns the joint IDs; unit tests with fake drives
  • Compose override docker/docker-compose.sil.yml: robot_pc with the real hardware interface on the virtual bus, gripper as mock
  • dynamixel_hardware_interface configuration in smartmanipulator_x_description (port, baud, IDs 1–6, J2 pair, elbow gearbox), selected by hardware:=sil|real
  • robot.launch.py: hardware:=mock|sil|real; real stays refused until Stage 2
  • Run end to end with doppelstep native_sim and record the findings in the compatibility specification (SIL runs 1–10, 2026-11-15)
  • smx_smoke_test.sh against the SIL profile: PASS (2026-11-15); since SIL run 10 at 10 Hz with the bus behaving like the wire, no read timeouts
  • Operator PC (MoveIt 2) plans and executes against the SIL Robot PC (SIL run 9, 2026-11-15)
  • SIL in CI: decided against (2026-11-15), the job would take 20–30 min; SIL stays a local check (tutorial)

Exit: the Operator PC plans and executes a trajectory; the doppelstep sims follow it; smoke test green.

docs.title: Stage 2: one B-G431B-ESC1 on the bench (PC, ST-LINK VCP)
docs.text:
• docker-compose.hw.yml points at the ST-LINK VCP device (one joint, others mock)
  • Verify the maximum VCP baud rate and USB latency against D8
  • Give the drive its joint ID and 1 Mbps with smx_drive_setup.py
  • Bring up the drive with the doppelstep bring-up checklist (dead time first)
  • Verify Control Table accesses and timing used by dynamixel_hardware_interface (Sync/Bulk Read, Fast Sync Read) on real hardware; RTT logging in parallel
  • Note: the VCP is a full-duplex bridge, so this stage tests the protocol and timing, not the single-wire physical layer; test the single-wire.overlay build separately with a half-duplex USB adapter (U2D2, or a 3.3 V USB-UART with a half-duplex hookup) and a logic analyzer for the turnaround

Exit: one real joint follows trajectories from the Operator PC; compatibility spec rows set to Verified.

docs.title: Stage 3: Robot PC on the CM4-Duino
docs.text:
• Multi-arch image (docker buildx, linux/amd64 + linux/arm64) published to GHCR by docker-publish.yml
  • deploy/cm4-duino/: config.txt fragment (dtoverlay=disable-bt, UART, USB if needed), udev rule for /dev/ttyDXL, systemd unit that starts Compose, provisioning script
  • Compose profile hw-cm4 and per-target hardware config (sim, sil, hw-pc, hw-cm4) so port, baud and IDs are not hard-coded in launch files
  • Bus interface on the Arduino header (3.3 V UART to single-wire bus, motor power distribution); first on a breadboard, later possibly a shield in its own hardware repo
  • Fast DDS profile for Wi-Fi (unicast peers instead of multicast if discovery is unreliable)

Exit: the CM4 boots, starts robot_pc automatically and drives the bench joint from the Operator PC over Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Stage 4: full arm, two hosts
docs.text:
• All six doppelstep drives on the arm (gripper: separate project, D9)
  • Operator PC on a second computer over Wi-Fi (two-host operation)
  • Measure bus noise next to the stepper drives; decide TTL vs. RS-485 (D7)
  • Measure joint limits and replace the URDF placeholders

Exit: full pick-and-place demo; README status checklist complete.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Done on 2026-11-15: the documentation describes the doppelstep / CM4-Duino architecture, including the wiring. Remaining: the Operator PC README still describes the old controller. The current state of every item is on the project status page.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Linux UART timing on the CM4 (turnaround, latency) breaks DXL return timing Hardware half-duplex / auto-direction interface, never GPIO direction switching from user space; check Return Delay Time DDS discovery over Wi-Fi is unreliable or slow Unicast Fast DDS profile, fixed IP for the CM4 Stepper drive noise on a TTL bus Short wiring, common ground star point, RS-485 fallback (D7) ST-LINK VCP limits baud rate or adds latency Separate USB-UART adapter (D6) Single USB port on the CM4-Duino Keep the joint bus on the PL011 UART; USB stays free

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
The Robot PC owns the real-time-facing ROS 2 control path and is the only computer connected to the DYNAMIXEL bus:

ros2_control
  -> ROBOTIS dynamixel_hardware_interface
  -> DynamixelSDK
  -> /dev/ttyDXL (CM4 UART0 on the robot; virtual bus or USB serial port during development)
  -> doppelstep drives, IDs 1-6
  -> stepper motors

The stock ROBOTIS hardware interface is the intended path, but it must not be assumed compatible until the protocol and Control Table accesses have been checked against the current Jazzy source and doppelstep. See the compatibility specification. On the robot the Robot PC is a CM4 on the CM4-Duino board, see Robot PC on the CM4-Duino.

docs.title: Host and container
docs.text:
The Robot PC runs in Docker on any host with Docker Engine and Docker Compose v2; on the robot that host is Raspberry Pi OS on the CM4. The paths below (docker/, ros2_ws/, ros2_robot.repos) are in this repository. The current docker/ profile is based on ros:jazzy-ros-base. It imports the DYNAMIXEL SDK/interface dependencies through ros2_robot.repos and builds the project-owned packages; docker-compose.hw.yml maps a serial device (SMX_SERIAL_DEVICE) into the container with the dialout group.

MoveIt 2, RViz2, Gazebo, and the Operator PC application are intentionally excluded from this image. The Operator PC owns those dependencies and connects over ROS 2 DDS.

docs.title: Simulation on one computer
docs.text:
Until the hardware path is verified, the Robot PC runs with mock_components/GenericSystem: the commanded joint position becomes the state at once, so the whole ROS side (DDS, controllers, MoveIt on the Operator PC) can be developed without any drive. Everything runs in containers on one computer; a Docker network replaces the Wi-Fi link:

 one computer (Docker)
 ┌─────────────────────────────── smx_net 10.77.0.0/24 ───────────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                                    │
 │ robot_pc 10.77.0.10         probe (dynamic IP)      Operator PC container          │
 │ robot_state_publisher       ros2 CLI                MoveIt 2, RViz2                │
 │ ros2_control_node (mock)    smx_smoke_test.sh       (Operator PC repo)             │
 │ joint_state_broadcaster                                                            │
 │ arm_controller                                                                     │
 │ gripper_controller                                                                 │
 └──────────────────────── ROS 2 DDS, UDPv4, ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42 ────────────────────────┘

From the repository root (the getting started guide walks through it):

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up --build robot_pc                 # Robot PC
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh    # second host
File Role docker/docker-compose.yml robot_pc service (mock hardware by default), probe service (profile tools), network smx_net docker/docker-compose.sil.yml Override for the SIL setup: virtual DYNAMIXEL bus to simulated doppelstep drives, hardware:=sil docker/docker-compose.hw.yml Override that passes a serial device into the container (Linux hosts) docker/env.example Template for docker/.env: ROS_DOMAIN_ID, subnet, Robot PC address, image tag, serial device docker/dds/fastdds_udp.xml Fast DDS profile: UDPv4 only, no shared memory between containers smartmanipulator_x_bringup/launch/robot.launch.py robot_state_publisher, ros2_control_node, controller spawner; hardware:=mock (default), sil or real (refused until the bench stage) smartmanipulator_x_config/config/controllers.yaml joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller (J1–J5), gripper_controller, 100 Hz smartmanipulator_x_description/ Moveo model generated from the BCN3D CAD (tools/cad/) and its ros2_control block tools/diagnostics/smx_smoke_test.sh Discovery, controller state, and trajectory check from another host tools/sim/smx_dxl_bus.py, tools/sim/smx_sil_start.sh, tools/sim/smx_bus_timing.py Virtual DYNAMIXEL bus, start script of the SIL setup, bus timing diagnostics

docs.title: Joint contract
docs.text:
The Operator PC, the simulation, and the real hardware must use the same joint names. These are defined in smartmanipulator_x_description:

Joint Moveo axis DYNAMIXEL ID Controller j1_base J1 base 1 arm_controller j2_shoulder J2 shoulder 2 and 3 (two mirrored motors) arm_controller j3_elbow J3 elbow 4 arm_controller j4_forearm_roll J4 forearm roll 5 arm_controller j5_wrist J5 wrist 6 arm_controller gripper gripper servo (separate project; mock until then) 7 gripper_controller

Lengths, joint axes, and meshes come from the BCN3D Moveo CAD (BCN3D Moveo mechanics); joint limits are placeholders until measured on the arm. The gripper also has mimic joints (gripper_idler_gear, gripper_pivot_*, gripper_finger_*) that follow gripper; they are not in ros2_control. On the real robot, dynamixel_hardware_interface can map the two shoulder motors onto one joint with its transmission_to_joint_matrix and joint_to_transmission_matrix parameters; this is still to be configured and verified.

docs.title: SIL: simulated doppelstep drives
docs.text:
Status (2026-11-15): works end to end with six doppelstep native_sim drives; smx_smoke_test.sh passes, and since SIL run 10 the drives handle the shared bus themselves, without help from the virtual bus. Findings of all runs are in the compatibility specification. Stage 1 of the integration plan.

New to SIL? Follow the step-by-step tutorial.

In the SIL setup (software in the loop) the Robot PC uses its real hardware path, dynamixel_hardware_interface and DynamixelSDK, but the drives are the doppelstep firmware running on the PC as Zephyr native_sim. A small tool joins them into one virtual DYNAMIXEL bus:

 robot_pc container                                     Docker host (Linux or WSL 2)
 ros2_control -> DynamixelSDK -> /dev/ttyDXL (pty)
                                  smx_dxl_bus.py  ── TCP 5555 ──> doppelstep native_sim (ID 1)
                                                  ── TCP 5556 ──> doppelstep native_sim (ID 2)
                                                  ...         ──> ... (ID 6)
  • The virtual bus behaves like the wire. Every byte the host sends goes to all drives; only the addressed drive answers. What a drive sends reaches the host and the other drives, so a drive hears the status packet of the drive before it. The host does not receive an echo of its own packets, like with the bus interface of the CM4-Duino.
  • The drives take turns: in a Sync Read or Bulk Read each one answers after the status packet of the ID before it. A Fast Sync/Bulk Read of several drives stays unanswered (one drive cannot build the chained answer of all), and the ROBOTIS interface falls back to normal Sync Read after 10 attempts: expect ten FastSyncRead TxRx failed lines at start. Both need doppelstep with the X430 emulator 1.1.0 (SIL run 10). For older firmware the bus can do it instead: SMX_SIL_BUS_ARGS=--fast-read drop --read-order request in docker/.env (runs 2 and 3).
  • smx_bus_timing.py measures PING and Sync Read answer times on the bus, for diagnosing timeouts.
  • Timing: Zephyr native_sim emulates the UART interrupt of a drive with a thread that wakes every 10 ms, so with six drives taking turns a Sync Read takes up to about 65 ms instead of well under 1 ms. In the control loop the hardware interface waits for an answer for one control period only (setPacketTimeout(period_ms)), so SIL runs the controllers at 10 Hz (SMX_UPDATE_RATE, period 100 ms); at 25 Hz a few Sync Reads per second time out (SIL run 8, run 10). baud_rate 9600 (SMX_BAUD_RATE) only lengthens the DynamixelSDK timeout of the reads at start; the virtual bus ignores the baud rate. The bus reports each incomplete read (read incomplete: missing ID …) and a timing summary every 10 s. The communication error timeout of the interface is 5 s in SIL (500 ms otherwise), long enough for the 10 Fast Sync Read attempts before the fallback. The real bus keeps 100 Hz and 1 Mbps.
  • The simulated drives keep running between Robot PC starts. If a run was killed, they may still have torque on; in SIL the hardware interface therefore switches torque off at start (disable_torque_at_init). With hardware:=real it refuses to start instead, which is the safe behaviour on the arm.
  • A freshly started drive answers on the factory ID 1; the tool first moves each drive to its joint ID (--assign-ids), over that drive's own connection.
  • The gripper stays on mock hardware (separate project).
  • The controller manager takes its robot description, and with it the hardware, from /smx/robot_pc/control_description, which only robot.launch.py publishes. On the shared /robot_description another host (MoveIt on the Operator PC) could otherwise make it load mock hardware (SIL run 10). Check with ros2 control list_hardware_components.

On the real bus every drive needs its joint ID and the bus baud rate once (decision D8, 1 Mbps); a new drive answers on ID 1 at 57600 bps. Connect one drive at a time and run smx_drive_setup.py --port /dev/ttyDXL --id <joint ID> (in the Robot PC image, or tools/diagnostics/ of this repository). With --tcp localhost:5555 it does the same for one simulated drive.

Start the six simulated drives from the doppelstep repository (getting started), one per terminal or in the background:

# in the sfs-doppelstep repository (WSL 2 or Linux, Docker); the first time:
docker compose build
docker compose run --rm zephyr bash scripts/west-init.sh
# build the drive (again after a firmware change):
docker compose run --rm zephyr west build -b native_sim/native/64 -s app -d build-native
# six drives, each in its own container with its own flash file and bus link:
for i in 0 1 2 3 4 5; do
  docker compose run -d --rm --name dxl$((i+1)) -p $((5555+i)):5555 zephyr \
    python3 tools/sim/run_native.py run --tcp 5555 --link /tmp/ttyDXL -- --flash=/tmp/flash.bin
done
# stop them: docker stop dxl1 dxl2 dxl3 dxl4 dxl5 dxl6

--link and --flash keep the instances apart: by default all of them would use the same bus link and flash file in the shared build directory, and an ID written to one drive would land in the flash of the others.

Stop a Robot PC that still runs with mock hardware first: both use the robot_pc service and its fixed address. Then start the Robot PC with the SIL override, and check it as usual from a second host:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml up --build robot_pc
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh

For one-off commands in the image (xacro, ls, connection checks) use the probe service: docker compose run robot_pc fails with Address already in use while the Robot PC runs, because of the fixed address.

SMX_SIL_DEVICES and SMX_SIL_IDS in docker/.env change the addresses and IDs, for example to start with one drive: SMX_SIL_DEVICES=host.docker.internal:5555 and SMX_SIL_IDS=1 (the other joints then have no drive and the hardware interface reports them missing). On a Linux host without Docker Desktop, host.docker.internal is mapped to the host by extra_hosts.

The arm configuration for sil and real is in smartmanipulator_x_description/urdf/smartmanipulator_x.ros2_control.xacro: IDs 1–6, extended position mode, ID 3 mirrored, and transmission matrices that map the two shoulder drives onto j2_shoulder and include the 57/11 elbow gearbox. The values still to confirm in SIL are listed in the compatibility specification.

docs.title: Operator PC on the same network
docs.text:
The Operator PC container joins the network by name. In its Compose file:

services:
  operator_pc:
    environment:
      ROS_DOMAIN_ID: "42"
      RMW_IMPLEMENTATION: rmw_fastrtps_cpp
      FASTDDS_DEFAULT_PROFILES_FILE: /etc/smx/fastdds_udp.xml  # copy of docker/dds/fastdds_udp.xml
    networks: [smx_net]
networks:
  smx_net:
    external: true

Start the Robot PC first; it creates smx_net. On Windows, run the Operator PC container from a WSL 2 distribution so RViz2 can use WSLg (mount /tmp/.X11-unix and /mnt/wslg, pass DISPLAY, WAYLAND_DISPLAY, and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR). ROS 2 installed natively on Windows does not discover containers on smx_net: Docker Desktop does not route multicast between the host and its container networks.

docs.title: Moving to the robot
docs.text: The image has no host-specific state. On the CM4 (arm64) it is pulled as a multi-architecture image, and smx_net is replaced by the real network (Wi-Fi): drop the networks entries and use network_mode: host. ROS_DOMAIN_ID and the Fast DDS profile stay the same. The planned deployment is described in Robot PC on the CM4-Duino.

docs.title: Hardware shell
docs.text:
Build and start an interactive Robot PC shell with a serial device from the repository root:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.hw.yml run --rm robot_pc bash

On a development PC the device is the ST-LINK virtual COM port of a doppelstep board (typically /dev/ttyACM0) or a USB-UART adapter; on the robot it is /dev/ttyDXL. Set SMX_SERIAL_DEVICE in docker/.env (template: docker/env.example) to the device path and make sure the host user may open it. Docker Desktop on Windows does not pass a COM port into a Linux container; use a Linux host, or usbipd-win with WSL 2.

Inside the container, inspect the available packages with:

ros2 pkg list | grep -E '^(dynamixel_sdk|dynamixel_interfaces|dynamixel_hardware_interface|smartmanipulator_x_)'

robot.launch.py refuses hardware:=real until the real-hardware path is verified in SIL and on the bench (Stages 1 and 2 of the integration plan). No physical bring-up is validated yet.

docs.title: Network and operation
docs.text:
The Robot PC communicates with the Operator PC using ROS 2 DDS over the configured network. Configure the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID on both computers and validate DDS discovery, selected network interfaces, multicast/unicast policy, and firewall behavior on the actual network. Do not use SSH as the ROS transport.

Do not enable motor motion until the actuator mapping, motor-driver configuration, limits, homing behavior, and an appropriate stop/safety procedure have been reviewed on the assembled robot. Test incrementally: mock hardware, simulated drives (SIL), one drive on the bench, one physical joint, then the complete mechanism.

docs.title: Repository ownership
docs.text:
• Robot PC Docker and bringup: docker/ and ros2_ws/src/smartmanipulator_x/smartmanipulator_x_bringup/.
  • Project controller and hardware configuration: ros2_ws/src/smartmanipulator_x/smartmanipulator_x_config/.
  • Canonical robot description location: ros2_ws/src/smartmanipulator_x/smartmanipulator_x_description/.
  • Upstream dependencies: separate source checkouts selected by ros2_robot.repos; pin immutable revisions for reproducible builds before production use.

docs.title: Robot PC on the CM4-Duino
docs.text:
On the robot, the Robot PC will be a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 on a CM4-Duino carrier board. It will run the same Robot PC image as the development PC, built for arm64, and reach the Operator PC over Wi-Fi.

Status (2026-11-15): planned (Stage 3 of the integration plan). Nothing on this page is implemented yet; it is the target the work is measured against.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
CM4-Duino + CM4 (Wi-Fi, eMMC)
 ├── Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (64-bit) + Docker Engine + Compose v2
 ├── systemd unit smx-robot.service  -> docker compose up robot_pc
 └── robot_pc container (ghcr.io/systemfromscratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot, arm64)
       ros2_control -> dynamixel_hardware_interface -> DynamixelSDK -> /dev/ttyDXL
                                                                     -> DYNAMIXEL bus -> doppelstep × 6

ROS 2 lives only in the container, so the host OS can stay Raspberry Pi OS (best hardware support for the CM4 and the board) even though ROS 2 Jazzy targets Ubuntu 24.04.

docs.title: Bring-up checklist (planned)
docs.text:
1. Flash Raspberry Pi OS to the eMMC (CM4-Duino), set host name, user, Wi-Fi and SSH.
  2. Run deploy/cm4-duino/provision.sh, reboot.
  3. Check /dev/ttyDXL exists and the serial console is off.
  4. Connect one doppelstep drive through the bus interface; ping it with DynamixelSDK or DYNAMIXEL Wizard.
  5. Start smx-robot.service; run the smoke test from the Operator PC.

docs.title: Tutorial: checking SIL step by step
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through a complete SIL check (software in the loop) of the Robot PC: the real ROS 2 control path (ros2_control, the ROBOTIS dynamixel_hardware_interface, DynamixelSDK) talks to six simulated doppelstep drives instead of motors. You need no electronics, only a PC.

Status (2026-11-15): SIL works end to end and smx_smoke_test.sh passes. Since SIL run 10 the drives share the bus like on the wire (they take turns themselves), the controllers run at 10 Hz, and after the start there are no failed reads and no overruns (see known limitations). New to all this? Start with the beginner tutorial. Stage 1 of the integration plan.

What you will have at the end: six virtual drives on IDs 1–6, the Robot PC with all controllers active, a test trajectory that completes, and a log that you can read and judge yourself.

Time: about 30 minutes the first time (mostly builds), 2 minutes later.

 Terminal 1-6 (doppelstep)        Terminal 7 (Robot PC)                Terminal 8 (checks)
 drive ID 1 .. ID 6               robot_pc container                   probe container
 native_sim, TCP 5555..5560  <──  smx_dxl_bus.py ── /dev/ttyDXL  <──  ros2_control   <── smx_smoke_test.sh

How the parts fit together is described in Robot PC → SIL.

docs.title: Step 0: Check the prerequisites
docs.text:
What Why Check Linux, or Windows with WSL 2 (e.g. Ubuntu) doppelstep native_sim and the pty bus need Linux wsl -l -v in PowerShell shows VERSION 2 Docker Desktop with WSL integration enabled for your distribution (or Docker Engine on Linux) both repositories build and run in containers docker version inside WSL shows a client and a server git and python3 in WSL clone the repositories, run the bus tests git --version, python3 --version (3.10 or newer) about 10 GB of free disk space ROS 2 and Zephyr images

\"The command 'docker' could not be found in this WSL 2 distro\"

In Docker Desktop open Settings → Resources → WSL integration, enable your distribution, press Apply & restart, then open a new WSL terminal.

wsl opens docker-desktop instead of Ubuntu

Docker Desktop installs its own distribution docker-desktop, which has no bash. If wsl -l -v marks it with * (default), open your distribution by name, for example wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04, or make it the default once with wsl --set-default Ubuntu-24.04.

Python on WSL

If python3 is missing: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3. The SIL tools use only the Python standard library; nothing has to be installed with pip.

All commands below run in WSL terminals (or in a Linux shell), not in PowerShell.

docs.title: Step 1: Get both repositories
docs.text:
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-doppelstep.git doppelstep
git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot.git

You can also use an existing clone on the Windows drive, for example /mnt/c/.../SmartManipulator-X-Robot-PC. In this tutorial ROBOT stands for the Robot PC repository and DOPPEL for the doppelstep repository. Set them once in every new terminal:

export ROBOT=~/sfs-smartmanipulator-x-robot
export DOPPEL=~/doppelstep

docs.title: Step 2: Test the virtual bus (1 minute)
docs.text:
The tool tools/sim/smx_dxl_bus.py joins the drives into one bus. Its tests use fake drives, so they show whether the bus itself works on your PC:

cd "$ROBOT/tools/sim"
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

Expected: OK at the end (14 tests at the time of writing). On Windows outside WSL the pty tests are reported as skipped; that is why this tutorial uses WSL.

docs.title: Step 3: Build the simulated doppelstep drive
docs.text:
The first time, build the toolchain image and fetch Zephyr into its Docker volume:

cd "$DOPPEL"
docker compose build
docker compose run --rm zephyr bash scripts/west-init.sh

Then build the drive (again after every change to the firmware):

cd "$DOPPEL"
docker compose run --rm zephyr west build -b native_sim/native/64 -s app -d build-native

The first time takes several minutes. Expected: the build ends with a zephyr.exe in build-native/zephyr/. Details are in the doppelstep getting started guide.

docs.title: Step 4: Test one drive on its own
docs.text:
Start one drive and talk to it with the doppelstep smoke test before you start six:

cd "$DOPPEL"
docker compose run -d --rm --name dxl1 -p 5555:5555 zephyr \
  python3 tools/sim/run_native.py run --tcp 5555 --link /tmp/ttyDXL -- --flash=/tmp/flash.bin
sleep 3
python3 tools/sim/dxl_smoke_test.py --tcp localhost:5555

Expected: the smoke test reports success; the drive answers PING with model number 1020, the XM430-W350 it emulates. Leave dxl1 running.

docs.title: Step 5: Start all six drives
docs.text:
cd "$DOPPEL"
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  docker compose run -d --rm --name dxl$((i+1)) -p $((5555+i)):5555 zephyr \
    python3 tools/sim/run_native.py run --tcp 5555 --link /tmp/ttyDXL -- --flash=/tmp/flash.bin
done
docker ps --filter name=dxl --format '{{.Names}}  {{.Ports}}'

Expected: six containers dxl1 … dxl6 on ports 5555 … 5560.

Every drive starts on the factory ID 1. You do not change that yourself: the bus moves each drive to its joint ID when the Robot PC starts. Each instance has its own flash file (--flash) and bus link (--link), so an ID written to one drive does not land in the others.

docs.title: Step 6: Start the Robot PC in SIL mode
docs.text:
If a Robot PC with mock hardware is still running, stop it first (both use the same service and fixed address):

cd "$ROBOT"
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml down

Start the Robot PC with the SIL override, in its own terminal; it stays in the foreground and shows the log:

cd "$ROBOT"
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml up --build robot_pc

docs.title: Step 7: Read the start log
docs.text:
Wait for Configured and activated gripper_controller. On the way you should see these lines, in this order. Tick them off:

  • [smx_dxl_bus] INFO connected to host.docker.internal:5555 … :5560: the bus reaches all six drives.
  • ID 1 present (model 1020) … ID 6 present (model 1020): each drive is on its joint ID.
  • bus up: /dev/ttyDXL -> /dev/pts/…, 6 drive(s): the serial device for the host exists.
  • port_name /dev/ttyDXL / baudrate 9600: the hardware interface uses the SIL settings.
  • Ping succeeded. Dynamixel model number : 1020 for IDs 1–6.
  • item_name: Drive Mode data: 1 for ID 3 only (the mirrored shoulder drive).
  • Ten lines FastSyncRead TxRx failed (attempt n/10), then switching to normal SyncRead permanently. This is expected: a doppelstep drive does not answer a Fast Sync Read that lists other drives too (it cannot build their part of the answer), and the interface falls back to normal Sync Read.
  • Loaded hardware 'SmartManipulatorXArm' from plugin 'dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware': the arm runs on the drives, not on mock hardware.
  • Torque ON for IDs 1–6, then Dynamixel Hardware Start!.
  • Configured and activated joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller.

Could not enable FIFO RT scheduling policy is a harmless warning: the container runs without real-time privileges.

docs.title: Step 8: Run the smoke test
docs.text:
In a second terminal:

cd "$ROBOT"
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe smx_smoke_test.sh

The test runs in the probe container, a second ROS 2 host on the same Docker network, the way the Operator PC will connect later. It checks four things:

  1. /joint_states arrives from the Robot PC.
  2. joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller are active.
  3. A test trajectory (out and back, 4 s) on arm_controller ends with SUCCEEDED.
  4. The joint positions after the trajectory.

Expected: PASS on the last line. The trajectory went through DynamixelSDK, the virtual bus and the doppelstep firmware of six drives, and the positions came back the same way.

docs.title: Step 9: Try it yourself
docs.text:
All commands run in the probe container. Open a shell there:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm probe bash

Look at the joint states (values in radians):

ros2 topic echo --once /joint_states

Move one joint, for example the base (j1_base) by 0.5 rad in 3 s and back:

ros2 action send_goal /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory \
  control_msgs/action/FollowJointTrajectory \
  "{trajectory: {joint_names: [j1_base, j2_shoulder, j3_elbow, j4_forearm_roll, j5_wrist],
    points: [{positions: [0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0], time_from_start: {sec: 3}},
             {positions: [0, 0, 0, 0, 0],   time_from_start: {sec: 6}}]}}"

Check the controllers and the hardware:

ros2 control list_controllers
ros2 control list_hardware_components

j2_shoulder drives two drives (IDs 2 and 3) and j3_elbow includes the 57/11 gearbox: the transmission matrices printed at start (transmission_to_joint_matrix_) show this mapping.

docs.title: Step 10: Save and judge the log
docs.text:
After about 30 s of running, save the log of the Robot PC:

cd "$ROBOT"
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml logs --no-color robot_pc > sil_run.log 2>&1

Count the messages that matter:

grep -c "FastSyncRead TxRx failed" sil_run.log   # expected: 10 (the fallback at start)
grep -c "\] SyncRead Rx Fail" sil_run.log         # failed normal Sync Reads, expected: 0
grep -c "Overrun detected" sil_run.log            # control cycles longer than 100 ms, expected: 0
grep "read incomplete" sil_run.log | head         # which drive did not answer in time
grep "\[smx_dxl_bus\] INFO reads:" sil_run.log    # bus summary every 10 s

How to read them:

Message Meaning Acceptable now? FastSyncRead TxRx failed, 10 times fallback to Sync Read at start yes, expected SyncRead Rx Fail / Dynamixel Read Fail (Duration: … ms/5000ms) a read timed out (after one control period); the interface keeps the last values and retries in the next cycle should not appear at 10 Hz; if it does, check that SMX_UPDATE_RATE is not set higher in docker/.env. The run fails only if the duration reaches 5000 ms Overrun detected … 10 Hz one cycle took more than 100 ms single ones at start are harmless; regular ones are not expected read incomplete: missing ID n after x ms the bus line for the same event: which ID was missing, and after how long the host gave up for diagnosis reads: … last answer after p50 / p95 / max how long the drives take to answer, one after the other for diagnosis; about 45 / 60 / 65 ms with six simulated drives

The log stays in your repository folder; it is not committed (delete it when you are done, or attach it to an issue).

docs.title: Step 11: Stop everything
docs.text:
cd "$ROBOT"
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml -f docker/docker-compose.sil.yml down
docker stop dxl1 dxl2 dxl3 dxl4 dxl5 dxl6

The drives can also keep running between Robot PC starts: a new Robot PC finds them again, and in SIL it switches off torque that an earlier run left on.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Timing of the simulated drives. Zephyr native_sim emulates the UART interrupt of a drive with a thread that wakes every 10 ms. The drives answer a Sync Read one after the other, so a read of six drives takes up to about 65 ms instead of well under 1 ms on the real bus. In the control loop the hardware interface waits for the answers for one control period only, whatever the baud rate, so SIL runs the controllers at 10 Hz (100 ms). At 25 Hz (40 ms) a few Sync Reads per second time out (SIL run 10). You can try another rate with SMX_UPDATE_RATE in docker/.env.
  • Fast Sync Read is not used with several drives: one drive cannot build the chained answer of all, so it stays silent and the interface uses normal Sync Read. On the real bus at 1 Mbps a Sync Read of six drives takes about 1.5 ms (calculated: six status packets of 21 bytes plus the request), so this costs little.
  • The gripper stays on mock hardware; it is a separate project (virtual DYNAMIXEL on ID 7).
  • SIL checks the protocol and the control path, not the mechanics: there is no real motor, load or friction behind a simulated drive.
